TL;DR Months to years of planning for the inevitable is not price fixing.

Not price fixing... illegal price fixing involves some sort of backroom communication between "competitors." The reality is that these companies have very large marketing departments full of people that can and do work around the clock to keep up with "changes in market conditions." In addition, they all are usually working on or have made progress towards some form of what you see as a new product or service or pricing plan for a period of months if not years prior to its release.

Something as "simple" as moving to non-subsidy has impacts to many parts of the business: Finance has to build out new and change existing revenue models, adjust budgets and set targets. IT work must be completed augmenting billing and ordering systems to support (millions in cost and months of work). Marketing must develop new strategies; commercials, taglines, signage, training. Legal of course has to be involved, giving approval on pretty much everything customer facing. Then there are direct customer communications which may be necessary to fulfill regulatory requirements, which with 10's of millions of customers is no small or cheap task itself. In truth its a daunting project that requires the thought and efforts of hundreds of people.

For phone subsidies, in truth, carriers have been studying the possibility of eliminating them for several years if not at least a decade. The reason you are seeing all the carriers at least offer non-subsidy/contract options is because the cost of devices has increased many times over versus what was normal pre-2007 (iPhone.. which if you think about it was a hybrid situation itself where data plans were cheap and customer cost was very high). Even in the past 2-3 years, average cost has gone way up due to consumer's current love affair with ridiculously large phones.

With the subsidy model, and low equipment costs, carriers were able to bank on the idea that if they pay for $100-$200 they would easily get back that money in the form of profits from service costs in 12-18 months. It was never guaranteed, but it was a pretty sure bet. Even if customers never really understood how it worked, they were happy paying $0-$199 for a phone. Fast forward to the past couple of years and you now have equipment that requires $300-$400 subsidy to get to those magic, customer friendly $0-$199 prices. Service prices on the other hand have risen moderately, but certainly not by 2-3x. Then for icing on the cake, consider the added cost of replacing devices for warranty and insurance claims (which are now occurring more frequently because bigger phone=more surface area to damage).

What was once a sure bet is now a confusing and complicated game with low odds. So the best way to win becomes not to play and get out of subsidy all together. Moving to installment plans puts the cost squarely on the consumer, and allows the carrier to better categorize their cost (they are still paying up front btw) as debt/future income (which can mean big differences to what reports look like). It also gives them the opportunity to give existing costs/fees a new more friendly sounding coat of paint. What is now "no interest" and "no upgrade/activation fees" is rolled into increases in monthly charges throughout the length of your installment plan. Discounts are available, as long as you can keep your old phone in working order.

So its not price fixing, one CEO calling up another saying, "lets set the bottom of prices at X", its more like, "T-Mobile did a press-release on installment plans. Pass the word along, tell the men, its time to shoot the moon!" (aka launch that project we've been working on for years).
